claims.text: Applying a thin Mo-rich surface coating to boride-based components will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The Mo-rich coating will form a stable, passivating Mo-oxide layer.
A passivating Mo-oxide layer will inhibit attack by molten aluminum.
The intervention can be implemented by depositing a thin Mo-rich interlayer by sputtering or physical vapor deposition.
Approximately 660 °C is representative of typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures.
The coating will incorporate Mo atoms into the component's outer layer.
Mo incorporation into the outer layer will enable formation of a continuous Mo-oxide barrier.
The Mo-rich coating will oxidize in the high-temperature molten-aluminum environment.
The resulting Mo oxide will act as a diffusion barrier.
The proposed diffusion barrier will limit molten-aluminum attack on the underlying boride structure.
Mo-coated components will have lower corrosion current density than uncoated boride components under identical molten-aluminum conditions.
Mo-coated components will have less mass loss than uncoated boride components under identical molten-aluminum conditions.
Coating effectiveness will depend on coating thickness, adhesion, and stability.
An excessively thick Mo coating may suffer mechanical wear.
Temperatures or cyclic conditions beyond the Mo-oxide stability range may diminish protection.
Molybdenum can improve alloy passivation by contributing to a protective surface layer that limits corrosion.
Coated and uncoated samples will be exposed to molten aluminum at approximately 660 °C and compared using mass loss, electrochemical measurements, and surface analysis.

The hypothesis will be falsified if coated samples show no statistically significant reduction in both mass loss and corrosion-current indicators relative to controls, or if the anticipated stable oxide does not form.
